title: Given a number N (assume N >= 2), draw a flowchart to check whether it is prime and print Yes if prime, otherwise No. Start, read N, initialize i = 2 and isPrime = true, loop while i < N (or i*i <= N) doing if N % i == 0 then isPrime = false and break, i = i + 1, decision isPrime == true, Yes print Yes, No print No, End. Input: 7, Expected Output: Yes (e.g. 9 -> No).
shortTitle: Check Prime: check whether N is prime and print Yes or No
keyPoints: A prime number has no divisors from 2 to sqrt(N); checking up to sqrt(N) reduces cost from O(n) to O(sqrt(n)).
Use i * i <= N as the loop bound to avoid floating-point Math.sqrt and its rounding issues.
Break immediately on finding the first divisor: one factor is enough to decide composite.
Two is the only even prime; after checking two, loop only odd candidates starting at 3.
For numbers below 2, return not-prime immediately; 2 is the smallest prime.
For cryptographic-size primes, use BigInteger.isProbablePrime which runs Miller-Rabin internally.

s1_definition.oneliner: A number is prime if no integer from 2 up to its square root divides it evenly, and checking only up to the square root is the key efficiency.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Prime** – an integer > 1 with no positive divisors other than 1 and itself.
- **Square-root bound** – divisors come in pairs; if none up to sqrt(N), none exist at all.
- **Loop bound** – `i * i <= N` avoids floating-point sqrt.
- **Early break** – one divisor is enough to decide composite.
- **Even shortcut** – check 2 separately, then test only odd candidates.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India validates hashing parameters by checking they are prime, because prime moduli distribute values more evenly. The system checks whether 7 has any divisor from 2 to its square root, finds none, and confirms prime. 9 is divisible by 3, so it is rejected.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A prime number has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. To test primality, try dividing N by each candidate from 2 up to the square root. If any divides evenly, N is composite; otherwise it is prime. The square-root bound works because divisors come in pairs, and at least one member of each pair is at or below sqrt(N).

The flowchart sets a flag, loops the candidate divisor, sets the flag false and breaks on the first hit, then prints Yes or No based on the flag. Write the bound as `i * i <= N` to avoid a floating-point square root, and break immediately because one factor settles the answer.

For cryptographic-size primes, trial division is far too slow. Java's `BigInteger.isProbablePrime` runs Miller-Rabin internally and handles any size. Trial division is for small configuration parameters and interview demonstrations.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, hashing parameters were validated as prime to ensure even distribution. The PrimeChecker confirmed 7 and rejected 9.

Remember one sentence: test divisors only up to the square root, break on the first one found, and use `i * i <= N` to avoid floating-point math.
